utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. This is Wednesday, March 2nd, 2011. I greet the accused, counsel, members of the OTP, and everyone helping us, Court Officers, interpreters, ushers, and Registrar and security guards. I will give the floor to Mr. Scott who asked for it, and then we will start with our rejoinders. And it will be D3 that will start. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, each of Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, in light of the events yesterday, and I'm going to keep this very short, and I was prepared to say more but as I've considered it further this morning I'm going to say less rather than more, but there are two points that I do want to make, and I do want to make, as Mr. Karnavas sometimes says, the Prosecution record on this. In terms of the scope of rebuttal that was allowed to the Prosecution, Your Honours, reference was made to a Rule -- to a 2002 oral ruling by Judge Liu, a Trial Chamber ruling that in no way is binding on this Chamber. Rule 86(A) in no place on the face of the rule says anything about limiting rebuttal to "brand new material." There's nothing in the rule that says that. There's nothing in the Judge Liu ruling that specifically says that. And in any event, Judge Liu's ruling is not at all binding on this Chamber at all. Every point we attempted to address arose directly out of the Defence closing arguments. There was no reference to anything not made in the closing arguments, and we provided the Chamber on every occasion the record citation to where the Defence argument was made. We did not repeat what was in our -- what was in our brief but attempted to address matters which we felt we had not previously had the opportunity to address. It was not for the sole purpose of reinforcing the Prosecution case because it was directly in response to cited arguments made during the closing arguments. And finally, Your Honours, we were specifically guided. Last Thursday we stood up, we gave the Chamber the topics, there was discussion, Defence were heard, the Chamber ruled - and I didn't want to say yesterday because I wanted to go back and look specifically at the regard lest I possibly be mistaken in what the ruling was - the Trial Chamber said -- and when we left the courtroom last Thursday and when Mr. Stringer and I prepared our submissions since Thursday until last -- until yesterday morning, this is the trial ruling that we were governed by. That we were governed by. Transcript page 52185, the President: "We wish to remind the Prosecutor that during the three hours they should focus on the most important points only, especially those which in their view they had not discussed sufficiently." In the ruling. There was no ruling that it had to be limited -- it was limited to brand new matters. There was nothing to that effect. We were given three hours, and that was the guidance we were given. We prepared accordingly. I don't think, Your Honours, with great respect to the Chamber and my greatest respect, but I did feel the need to say this. I do not believe that the Prosecution was treated fairly yesterday at all and inconsistent with the guidance the Chamber gave us when it ruled on these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is now on the record. Let me remind the D3, D4, D5, and D6 Defences, before they take the floor, to tell us -- and when they take the floor to tell us, On such a page, the Prosecutor said this. And then you can give us your rejoinder so that we can actually follow in an efficient manner what you are saying. Mr. Kovacic, I see that you have the lectern. You asked for ten minutes and you have your ten minutes, and now you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. [In English] I will address only the issue of occupation, which was addressed by the Prosecution on the very beginning of their oral arguments yesterday. More precisely, it was -- more precisely, it was Mr. Stringer who discussed the issue. And for -- for better planning, Your Honours, I would like to inform you also that General Praljak will not address the Court on the end. Talking about this subject, I would like, first, to state only two basic points. First, the Prosecution strongly advocates that there was an armed conflict at all times and all places where the alleged crimes occurred. Defence claims that the HVO did not have effective control over the territory where armed conflict took place. There is no evidence that would support the Prosecution's claim. Second point: The local Croats won the democratic local elections and formed coalition municipal governments in municipalities encompassed by the indictment. Thus, the HZ-HB or HVO was not a foreign occupier. He held the power in those municipalities even before the conflict. On page -- regarding the statement of the Prosecution on daily page number 23 yesterday, occupation must be by foreign forces. The Prosecution still cannot bring themselves to say Croatia occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yesterday, the Prosecution stopped short of defining precisely who occupied the territories. Was it Republic of Croatia? Was it HV or the HVO or some combination of those? In final brief, the Praljak Defence never said, as Prosecution yesterday cited, foreign forces must occupy. We said that according to the international law, Republic of Croatia must have had effective control, the same kind of control they had over their own, own, armed forces. This is the required test, effective control. There is no evidence that would show existence of effective control in that case. The Prosecution suggest that Article 47 of Additional Protocol I is in response to avoiding duties of occupation. That is fine, but -- but that does not prove that Croatia occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not an argument in that direction. The Prosecution has failed to prove a foreign military occupation followed by a -- by a "puppet government." They have failed. And the reference to Article 47 is not helpful. The Prosecution makes reference to new secondary materials in rejoinder, not included in final brief except by an unexplained footnote. This is a flagrant abuse of process. That said, the secondary material referenced does not overthrow the fundamental fact that we need a foreign power with effective control. They referenced -- the Prosecution reference to Israel and Beirut doesn't exactly help. Israel's occupation of Lebanon could not be used as comparation -- for comparation. On page 25 and following, the Prosecutor deals with issue of state of occupation where there is armed -- existence of state of occupation where there is armed conflict. The Prosecution suggests that pockets of resistance does not negate occupation. This is a very small territory, he says. The question is: Is it really accurate to call these pockets of resistance? Is the Prosecution conceding that there was no armed conflict and thus no international armed conflict and thus no nexus to international armed conflict? They couldn't have both. Related to that, the Prosecution cited finding in Naletilic regarding Doljani and Sovici, but, in fact, this argument is favouring the Defence thesis, because in Naletilic the judgement deals only with April 1993 in those places, and in this case we heard that there were combat activities from April to September, particularly massacre of Croat population took place in that time as well. I will not go further in details, but the Chamber will recall that in summer and autumn of 1993, the HVO was under constant attack of ABiH. Thus are we really talking about the pockets of resistance? The combat is really still going on, so there cannot be state of occupation. General Praljak was not commanding general of occupied territory, and we said so before. He was a front-line officer of a domestic group preventing massive expulsion of Bosnians who happened to be ethnically Croatian. There is no evidence that General Praljak was the king of the territory. He was not even a gerent, as the Prosecution originally asserted. By the way, on that subject matter, we attempted to introduce evidence, a statement under Rule 92 bis, of Mr. Bennefeld [phoen], which was about transfer of Jews and other people from Sarajevo and human assistance provided to Sarajevo with assistance and help of HVO, particularly General Praljak, but that was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, I apologise for the interruption, but we object to references to non-evidence, that is, tendered 92 bis statements that are not in evidence. And this is also getting beyond the scope of the legal submissions made in respect of occupied territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I accept at that objection, but I'm just done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, please use the exhibits that are in evidence. Only use those who are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It wasn't necessary because it was my last sentence which is now cut off. So I should only add that Praljak was a volunteer, not a king. And I'm done. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Very well. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor. You gave us a document. I believe we'll have it on the screen. There are two columns to this document, and there is an explicit reference to the words of the Prosecution. And on the right-hand side column we have your answer, your analysis of these points. Thank you very much. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution and those from the Defence, as well as the accused and everybody else present in the courtroom and around it. Unfortunately, nothing will be shown on the screens because we had -- didn't have enough time to make a PowerPoint presentation for our rejoinder. But we have hard copies so that you, Your Honours, will have -- or have your respective copies, and I have also just given some to Mr. Stringer. So you'll be able to follow our rejoinder. By way of introduction, let me say that the time devoted by the Prosecution in its rebuttal to the Petkovic Defence to us is a confirmation of the relevance of the -- of closing arguments of the Petkovic Defence. We understand that as a compliment, and it is with pleasure that we reply to our learned friends from the Prosecution. Our first assertion is about what Mr. Stringer said on page 4 of the transcript, that it's up to the Prosecution to prove that the Muslim prisoners have the status of civilians. But in the very next sentence Mr. Stringer, in a way, contradicts himself. The Petkovic Defence wishes to stress that it does not dispute that some military-aged and able-bodied men may have been civilians, but it is a fact that such men are not considered civilians until proven otherwise. And it seems that we basically agree with the Prosecution on that. In this trial, this -- the Prosecution has not proved that military-aged able-bodied men who are considered victims and who are isolated in early July 1993 indeed were civilians. Our second point is Mr. Stringer's reference to the judgement in the Celebici case. We wish to say, with regard to that, that the Defences in the Celebici case argued that the prisoners in that detention centre were neither prisoners of war nor persons enjoying the protection of the Geneva Conventions. The Prosecution in that case initially argued that they were prisoners of war, which was not the position of the Defence. The Petkovic Defence is different from the position -- has a position different from that of the Defence in the Celebici case. We have prepared paragraph 243 of the judgement in that case from which you can see the position of the Defence in that case, but this surely is not relevant here. Mr. Stringer, furthermore, as noted on page 5 of yesterday's transcript, said that reservists are considered civilians until they are mobilised. We would like to draw your attention to document 4D1164, which is a decision on general mobilisation adopted by the Presidency of BH on 20 June 1992. Pursuant to that, all conscripts between the ages of 18 and 65 were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 55, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We add that this mobilisation was not abolished in 1993, which, according to the criteria stipulated by the Prosecution itself, the reservists in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the declaration of general mobilisation were not civilians any more. Our position is that they were the reserve force of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina even before that. On this same page, page 5, Mr. Stringer's assertion is recorded that reservists are not members of the armed forces. We appeal to the Trial Chamber to review the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, first and foremost the decree on the service in the BH Army, which is document 4D412. In this document, it is clearly stated that the BH Army consists of a standing and a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake on the transcript. Document is 4D1164 and not 4D412. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, it is not a mistake. Document 4D1164 is the decision of the Presidency of BH on general mobilisation, whereas now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. It was another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Your Honour. The following regulation of BH, the decree on military conscription, is 4D1030, in which it is clearly stated that all able-bodied men are subject to military conscription until the age of 60. From that, we follow, or we conclude: If the laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina state that the reservists are members of the BH Army, namely as that army's reserve force, then the Prosecution cannot claim the contrary, or at least they cannot argue against what is stated in the laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I repeat: They cannot dispute the status of reservists pursuant to laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On page 6, probably to corroborate their assertions, the Prosecution quoted General Petkovic, who said that when an HVO member on furlough rapes a Muslim woman, whether that is a crime that is connected with combat activity, to which General Petkovic answered in the negative, that such a member of the armed forces at that particular moment was a free civilian. We wish to point out that this was a relevant issue to establish a causal relationship between a crime and the armed conflict. The example of the crime of rape was used to point out under which circumstances such a crime is a war crime as opposed to the situation in which such a crime during a war can be merely a crime without the attribute "war," that is, not a war crime. So it was a matter which was relevant for the issue of nexus rather than for the status of the victim under international humanitarian law. Petkovic's opinion about the status of able-bodied men in Bosnia-Herzegovina has been put forward in this courtroom several times. General Petkovic was very clear: They were the reserve Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The other topic dealt with by Mr. Topic [as interpreted] were the Muslim soldiers of the HVO. Mr. Stringer additionally clarified the position of the Prosecution that the Muslim HVO soldiers are protected by international law based on Article 75 of Additional Protocol I. Our position is that Article 75 of the Additional Protocol does not apply, and we have elaborated on that in our final brief. We are not going to repeat it now. But we can add the following: The Prosecutor's position is not founded on international customary law. The Prosecution failed to give information about practice in any country, nor have they stated one relevant legal opinion in corroboration of their interpretation of Article 75. The Prosecution hasn't shown a precedent that would go to corroborate their position. As opposed to that, the Petkovic Defence can offer the following: Firstly, a quotation from the book by Antonio Cassese, "International Criminal Law," page 82. I quote: [In English] "War crimes may be perpetrated by military personnel against enemy servicemen or civilians or by civilians against either members of the enemy armed forces or enemy civilians, for instance, in occupied territory. Conversely, crimes committed by servicemen against their own military, whatever their nationality, do not constitute war crimes. Such offences may nonetheless fall within the ambit of the military law of the relevant belligerents." [Interpretation] End of quote. The case law which referred to is the judgement of the Special Tribunal for Sierra Leone, the RUF case. I'll point out three elements. First I quote: [In English] "The law of armed conflict does not protect members of armed groups from acts of violence directed against them by their own forces." [Interpretation] Quoting from paragraph 1451. Following quotation from paragraph 1452: [In English] "The law of international armed conflict regulates the conduct of combats vis-à-vis their adversaries and persons hors de combat who do not belong to any of the armed groups participating in the hostilities." [Interpretation] And the following quotation is from paragraph 1453: [In English] "The law of international armed conflict was never intended to criminalise acts of violence committed by own member of an armed group against another, such conduct remaining first and foremost the province of the criminal law of the states of the armed group concerned and human rights law. In our view, a different approach would constitute an inappropriate reconceptualization of a fundamental principle of humanitarian law. We are not prepared to embark on such an exercise." [Interpretation] End of quote. We also point out the Apilts [phoen] and Motosuke cases, which we have mentioned in our final brief and the Coric Defence also referred to that in their final brief. The third topic is about the so-called Mrksic duty. The Prosecution, on page 8, points out the difference between domestic legislation and de facto responsibility based on custody as well as control over the prisoners. On this occasion I would like to stress that the Petkovic Defence agrees that responsibility depends on the nature of the accused's duty, which can be determined both -- by both the de jure and the de facto situation. On page 12, the words of Mr. Stringer were recorded that Generals Petkovic and Praljak had custody and control over the prisoners when they were under the control of HVO units during the performance of forced labour. I would like to state that, to our minds, the Prosecution here clearly shows that Petkovic and Praljak did not have custody of the prisoners while they were in detention centres or in any other situation when they were not performing what is called here forced labour. Furthermore, we interpret that position in the following way: Issuing an order to take prisoners for forced labour is not the proof of custody and control of the said prisoners. An approval for the work of prisoners of war was subject to an approval by those who did have custody and control over the detainees, but what matters the most is this: In any case, this did not imply any authority with regard to the treatment of the prisoners. Therefore, we would like to emphasise once again: The Prosecution claims that prisoners, while they were in detention units, were not under the control of General Petkovic before the 24th of July, we suppose, and then General Praljak after that date. Therefore, we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to look at that assertion and bear that in mind when they decide on the charges from 12 to 17 of the indictment, which in concerns the -- which concerns the conditions of detention and inhumane treatment of prisoners in detention centres. On page 13, Prosecution reacted to our closing argument about them not pleading about what regulations delegated Petkovic to look after the detainees. And the Prosecution referred to their indictment in doing that. By that allegation, they again confirmed that they did not mention a single piece of regulation or an order by a superior that might have been issued to General Petkovic and that might have concerned the care of detainees in detention centres. The Prosecution thus confirms that such a regulation does not even exist, and they did not manage to prove their allegations from the indictment beyond any reasonable doubt. On -- at the end of page 13 and following, for the first time after five years the Prosecution proffered an assertion that an order issued by Mate Boban on the 15th of September, 1993, document number P5104, that that is an order which authorised General Petkovic to look after the detainees and bound General Petkovic to look after the detainees. Since that was the first time we ever heard such an assertion in the courtroom, I will give it a little bit more time. I would like to call up document P5104 in e-court. For you, Your Honours, I have a hard copy. This order issued by Mate Boban consists of seven bullet points. The first two bullet points refer to the HVO units. Bullet points 3 and 4 refer to detention centres. Bullet point 5 refers to humanitarian aid. Bullet point 6 refers to the work of UNPROFOR. And finally, bullet point 7 refers to the HVO Main Staff. "The HVO's Main Staff shall inform all subordinated commands and units of this order and provide for professional help in its implementation." Mate Boban's order was forwarded to two different places. The first one was the Defence Department, then the second one was the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I conclude, this order issued by Mate Boban was not forwarded to Petkovic. General Praljak also did not forward the order to General Petkovic. Based on this order, Petkovic was not authorised to do absolutely anything. Furthermore, this order means that the Main Staff was duty-bound to inform subordinated commands and units. However, it was not duty-bound to inform any of the detention centres which are referred to in bullet points 3 and 4. The reason is very simple. The Main Staff of the HVO and its then-commander, Mr. Slobodan Praljak, did not have any authorities over the detention centres. If we look at the order that General Praljak forwarded to HVO units, document number P5188 - Your Honours, you again have a hard copy of the document - we will see that General Praljak indeed did not forward Boban's order to any of the detention centres. He didn't forward that order because General Praljak did not have any authorities over those detention centres. And my final conclusion is this: By this order, the Main Staff of the HVO and its commander, Slobodan Praljak, or anybody else in the Main Staff, no authorities over the detention centres were transferred. The following sentence that I deem very important is recorded on page 17. This is my learned friend Stringer's assertion that it is irrelevant whether Petkovic had control over the detention centres. I repeat that we deem this assertion that Petkovic did not have authorities over the detention centre to be important and that it should be taken into account when deciding on the crimes relative to the detention centres. The Prosecution, furthermore, on the same page asserts that Petkovic and Praljak as well had custody and control over detainees during the so-called forced labour. The same assertion is recorded on page 12. And in addition -- in reference to that, we would like to state that these are factual matters that have to be proven on a case-by-case basis. And the assertions presented by Mr. Stringer are assertions that the Prosecution failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt in this case. What is most important for us is the Prosecutor's position that Petkovic did not have control over detention centres. Therefore, he could not be held responsible for the treatment of prisoners and situations that occurred in those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I apologise. That's a mischaracterisation of the Prosecution position. The Prosecution position is that in respect of the Mrksic duty, the question is about his control over prisoners. We say his responsibility over the detention centres is irrelevant in respect of the Mrksic duty, but that's not a concession that he didn't have control or responsibility in respect of the detention facilities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to briefly respond to Mr. Stringer's intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I'm somewhat surprised by your intervention, because we're here in an adversarial system. Somebody states a statement, the other one will respond. And the last to respond will be the Defence team. So if whenever you are on your feet because you don't like what is being said, we're going to be here for another few years. So let the Defence speak, because they have, as per rules, the final word. They are now in the stage of the rejoinder, matters of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will spend just a brief minute to reply to Mr. Stringer. If the Prosecution claims that Generals Praljak and Petkovic had custody and control over the detainees during forced labour and if this -- if this is the only claim that they have to make about custody and control, then it arises from that by some -- based on argument en contrario we can conclude that in any other -- they didn't have control or custody in any other situation. Whether our interpretation is correct or not, of course, will be judged by the Trial Chamber. I have very little time left, so I have to speed along. On page 18, in respect of the Mrksic duty, the Prosecution repeats that there is a responsibility when detainees are transferred to another body. We would like to draw your attention to the fact that the Prosecution didn't either claim or prove that Petkovic had ever personally arrested somebody and transferred that person on to another body for further custody. We claim further on that the Chief of the Main Staff did not have the authority to supervise and control detention centres, the wardens of those detention centres, or the staff. There is clear evidence that other institutions were authorised to control the treatment of detainees. Within this context, we would also like to say that the Prosecution's position on the Mrksic duty reminds us of the following situation: A judge who sentences somebody is also responsible for the treatment of the person that they sentenced to a prison centre. And the fourth topic that I would like to tackle is the topic of occupation. However, my learned friend Mr. Kovacic has already explained that very well. I'll skip that part. There is no need for me to add anything, because my learned friend Mr. Kovacic said everything that is relevant, in my opinion. And the following topic concerns occupation, commanders. The Prosecution still claims that a military commander in an occupied territory has the authorities vested in an occupation commander. All those -- nobody gave him any executive authorities. And the Prosecution referred to the Hostages case. We would like to state the following: Neither the Hostages case nor the High Command case or any other case for that matter or the customary law in general confirmed the Prosecutor's argument because, firstly, not every commander in an occupied territory is an occupying commander in the command sense of the word. Secondly, only those commanders who had been given executive authorities over the occupied territory are indeed occupying commanders. Thirdly, the Prosecutor had five years in these proceedings during which time he claimed that in Herceg-Bosna there were civilian authorities, that the civilian authorities had control over the army, and all of those assertions and evidence led in that sense directly challenge the claim that a military commander was the highest executive power in Herceg-Bosna. Or, as Mr. Kovacic, said that Praljak or Petkovic before him was king in Herceg-Bosna. We would like to add to that that Milivoj Petkovic was not a military commander; he was a Chief of Staff. The indictment does not charge Petkovic as an occupying commander. Therefore, the assertions presented today or over the past two months referring to occupying commanders are not a valid part of the Prosecution case. Those assertions are erroneous and they're not proven. What we deem important is to mention the fact that the Prosecution did not refer to the part of our closing arguments in which we argue that they are the ones who interpret the authorities of the occupying commander as an objective authority, which means that we agree with the Defence of General Petkovic that the responsibility of an occupying commander is one part of command responsibility pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute and that for the existence of this part of responsibility one needs to prove all the necessary elements as well as for all the other elements of command responsibility. The Article of the Statute is 7/3. And my final remark concerns the relationship between an armed conflict and occupation and the relationship between the two. My learned friend Mr. Kovacic explained that very well. I don't need to belabour the point. I just need to say that between the Prosecution and ourselves there is no difference. There's no dilemma that this matter has been properly regulated by all the existing regulations. Indeed, minor conflicts do not deny the state of occupation. However, widely spread conflicts and fighting do challenge the state of occupation. In his case in the indictment and while leading evidence, the Prosecution tried to prove that there were conflicts, that those conflicts were widespread and systematic, and that there was fierce fighting going on especially from the month of April until the -- April 1993 until the end of the relevant period. And finally I would like to conclude by saying this: The Prosecution did not manage to refute the allegations of Petkovic Defence or prove beyond any reasonable doubt Petkovic's responsibility. We again conclude that the Prosecution believes that Petkovic did not have authority over detention centres, that he was not in charge of the treatment of the detainees in those detention centres. This, Your Honours, ends my rejoinder to the Prosecutor's rebuttal. Is it now the moment for me to say something in reference to Jadranko Prlic's rebuttal, or shall I do that after the -- all the Defence teams are finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are on your feet, you may do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I must repeat, Ms. Alaburic, please control the speed of your speech because it does not all come across to us. And the poor interpreters are audibly suffering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will behave and I will be brief. Jadranko Prlic's Defence yesterday presented their rebuttal to our closing argument in its part which concerned the transit centre in Ljubuski, and this is recorded on pages 84 through 89 of yesterday's transcript. And if I may summarise the position of Jadranko Prlic's Defence, I would like to do it in the following way: Transit centres were set up in order to look after displaced Croats from Central Bosnia. And there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. There was one transit centre. So we're talking about one transit centre. We're talking about the Ljubuski transit centre. So if we're going to be correct, let's be correct. So if you're going to summarise, summarise me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, in order -- one minute. In order to avoid this type of problem, you had to quote precisely what had been said by Mr. Karnavas. This would have absolved him of the need to object, which is here inadequate anyway in a final rejoinder. So just quote him exactly and then you can state your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but, you know, it's increasingly clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's increasingly clear that the one party in this courtroom that doesn't have a right to be heard is the Prosecution. When Mr. Karnavas -- when Mr. Stringer got up to his feet a few moments ago, he was again closed down and said not to say anything. You haven't said anything to Mr. Karnavas, but -- so it's okay for Mr. Karnavas to object, it's okay for the Defence to go on and on about their responses, but not for the Prosecution to be heard. There's a double standard in this courtroom and it's a shame that it's at the end of this case. This is absurd. It's unfair, Your Honours. You can't treat the parties differently. You can't have one set of rules for the Defence and other set of rules for the Prosecution. When Mr. Stringer gets up and makes a reasonable objection, he's shouted down. Mr. Karnavas gets up and then you direct your criticism to Ms. Alaburic. It's completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think that what I said was misinterpreted. I said this to Ms. Alaburic: I said that if she had quoted exactly what had been said by Mr. Karnavas, this problem would not have arisen, as was the problem stated by Mr. Karnavas. I was telling Ms. Alaburic to give exact quotes, quotations, which has nothing to do with what you have just said. I was just reminding you, as was stated by the Trial Chamber and as was said to everybody, that when we came to rebuttals and rejoinders you had to give exact references as to transcript pages and quotations. So I think now Ms. Alaburic understood me and she's going to do what I told her to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I believe that the intervention was in order, and I will explain why I used a plural. On page 74, line 17, records as follows: Transit centres for prisoners of war. Therefore, Mr. Karnavas said, or at least that was how it was recorded, although he didn't say it, and that's the only reason why I used the plural form. And if there is a mistake in the transcript, I will correct myself. And when I summarise what my learned friend Mr. Karnavas said on those pages, I will say that the rebuttal refers to the Petkovic Defence claims about the transit centre in Ljubuski and their claim that that transit centre was also set up for prisoners of war. Our rejoinder is as follows: The Petkovic Defence does not deny the claims presented by the Prlic Defence about the transit centre in Ljubuski and about the need to look for those Croats who had been expelled from Central Bosnia. In our closing argument we referred to paragraphs 105 and 131 of the indictment relative to the charges about the crimes of deportation of Muslim civilians and detainees from Heliodrom in mid-July 1993. Those charges, as they are worded in the indictment and as they are defined in Annex A of the Prosecutor's final brief, directly concern the office for refugees and displaced persons as well as the civilian authorities of the HVO. They are directly defined as immediate and direct perpetrators of those alleged crimes. If I have carefully enough read the final briefs of other Defence teams, the Prlic Defence team did not deal with any of the documents that concern the charges relative to the -- to mid-July 1993. Therefore, I thought that it would be my professional obligation, and due to the lack of time and due to some other circumstances, I thought that I should present one single legal position and that is that the crime of illegal deportation can be committed only against civilians and not against prisoners of war. And that our interpretation of the law must be correct, and that's why I need to say that it is not disputable that prisoners of war cannot be victims of crimes against humanity pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute, but they have to be part of systematic and widespread attack against a civilian population. Our position was based on several pieces of evidence. Let me quote some of them without mentioning those that the Prosecution mentioned in his Annex A. The documents in question are P3427; P3554; P3587; P3673; P3804; P3952; P9679; BA's testimony -- or, rather, the cross-examination by Prlic Defence of that witness on pages 7423 through 7429; testimony by Witness BC, both examination-in-chief and cross-examination by the Prlic Defence recorded on pages 18353 through 18355, as well as pages 18359 and 18595 through 18597. It was not our intention to harm anybody, but, rather, to say something that should be beneficial for all Defences. We don't think that we can be prejudicial to anybody, because according to the principles of the JCE, Milivoj Petkovic can be pronounced responsible for the actions of other persons and bodies, and this is all we have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I am now giving the floor to Mr. Coric's Defence. His counsel is to speak for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. On pages 8 and 9 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecutors assert that de jure it was Mr. Coric and the military police who had control over detention and prisoners. In this respect they cite two documents, P837 and P143. Both documents are instructions for the work of the military police. In both documents, in the section where the tasks of the military police are listed, under item (I) it says that the military police provides internal security in military prisons. And under item (T) it is stated that it participates in securing prisoners of war. Participates, Your Honour. So these two tasks are listed among their daily tasks. In their closing argument and its final brief, the Coric Defence has asserted and continues to assert that in the daily implementation of military police tasks the military police was de jure and de facto subordinated to military commanders. Furthermore, the mere securing of prisoners does not amount to running a prison. Running a prison includes control over wardens, visits, food, and releases. None of that -- none of these was done by the military police administration or Valentin Coric. It was all done by military commanders, for example, Colonel Obradovic or the Rama Brigade commanders. Let me give an example. The warden of Gabela was a member of the Knez Domagoj Brigade who was directly subordinated to Obradovic. And the prison wardens at Prozor were appointed by brigade commanders. All the details corroborated by evidence have extensively been dealt with by the Coric Defence in their final brief, and we won't repeat that now. On page 18 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution offers as a proven fact that prisoners were handed over to the military police, but the Prosecution failed to prove that assertion. The Coric Defence stands by its assertion, which they have corroborated by evidence during its closing argument, that prisoners were never, in fact, handed over to the military police, but, rather, that they stayed in the de facto custody of military commanders and under their control. This is not only asserted by the Coric Defence, Your Honours. Mate Boban knew that too. That is why in his document that we saw on the screens a short while ago, P5104, in item 7 he commands the Main Staff that they shall acquaint their subordinated units with that order and provide professional assistance in the implementation of that order. There is no item in that order in which Mate Boban says what the military police should do or the Military Police Administration or, indeed, the Department of Defence. On -- excuse me. I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to three more documents that corroborate how Mate Boban's order was forwarded. That's P5199, 1D1704, and 2D1319. I apologise to the interpreters. This was a digression. I'll return to my written speech. On page 10 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution speaks about the credibility of Prosecution Witness E. To support the credibility of that witness, the Prosecution refers to document P7411, which is a document issued by Mr. Pusic, as confirmation that the military police administration, the ODPR, Mr. Prlic, and the SIS took part in the programme of releasing persons from prison and is showing affidavits. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that neither Witness E nor the Prosecution, in connection with the releases in which this witness was involved, failed to mention any one of these bodies, and that is precisely one of the reasons, but only one of them, why the Coric Defence challenges the credibility of Witness E. Witness E and his documents testified to a practice that was very different. They mention none of these bodies. And they don't mention the way of releasing people as described in Mr. Pusic's document with which the whole story began. Some other persons are mentioned in connection with Witness E, such as some attorneys who have nowhere else, except in that one particular location, have been involved in any activities that have to do with the release of prisoners or the showing of affidavits. At the place where Witness E acted, the practice was unique and unorthodox. It was devised by Witness E of his own accord and in co-operation with some persons that were close to him. The military police administration or Valentin Coric or any one of the above-mentioned bodies, such as the ODPR, the SIS, or the exchange service, had nothing to do with that. On pages 9 and 10 of yesterday's transcript, the Prosecution cites document P7411, page 4, item 5, and say that the exchange service with the crime enforcement department of the military police and some other services grouped all prisoners together, which effected their release if they had all the required documents. Contrary to the assertions of the Prosecution, this document says that the exchange service compiled a list. And in that context, the crime enforcement department of the military police is not mentioned at all. The Coric Defence asserts, and continues to assert, and it is also corroborated by documents and witnesses we -- whom we have cited, that the crime enforcement service got these lists from the exchange service and some other bodies. That list -- on that list there were the names of some imprisoned persons. With regard to these names, the crime enforcement service was duty-bound to issue a certificate and forward it to these other bodies. This certificate only contained one piece of information, namely whether or not criminal proceedings are pending against that particular person from the list. That certificate did not contain information as to whether the person may or may not be released. Therefore, the crime enforcement service only provided such information as is given by the police anywhere in the world. The crime enforcement service did not decide about releases. I would also like to draw your attention to documents P4450 and 6D169. Thank you, Your Honours. The Coric Defence has finished. I would just like to point out that on page 27, line 15, after the -- after -- after the word exchange -- or the word exchange should be followed by the word "service." Exchange service, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor for the Pusic Defence. Mr. Pusic is not here, but he's represented. He's ill. So you have the floor for the last rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In our rejoinder we'll refer to transcript pages 52825 through 52827. Talking about advancing arguments, then I must say that what we heard yesterday from Mr. Stringer is just a repetition of what has already been -- had already been said in the final brief of the Prosecution and in the closing arguments of Mr. Kruger. We have heard nothing new that would justify advancing additional arguments. Namely, there must be some standards in place to allow advancing arguments in rebuttal. In our submission, these standards had not been met. What did Mr. Stringer do? He merely repeated what had been said by Mr. Kruger in his closing argument when he was accusing Mr. Pusic. Mr. Stringer even cited the same document as Mr. Kruger did in his closing argument. If we look at transcript page 52159, we see that Mr. Kruger cited the same document as Ms. Tomasegovic, and that is P7411. And it was cited again in this courtroom by Mr. Stringer. It's document P7411, which was mentioned by Mr. Kruger in his closing argument and again yesterday by Mr. Stringer. We don't understand why. Probably to reinforce their case as anticipated by Mr. Khan. It is a document which doesn't show that Mr. Pusic had any power or authority. It has been dealt with in the Prosecution final brief in paragraph 1248 and 1251, and it was documentary evidence which was not shown to any witness in this courtroom. Furthermore, Mr. Stringer cited Witness E's evidence, who was heard during the proceedings, but Mr. -- or Witness E's evidence cannot be linked to Mr. Pusic when it comes to the issuing of affidavits or letters of guarantee or the transfer to third countries. The Prosecution dealt with the evidence of this witness extensively in paragraph 1103 and 1106 of their final brief. Again, nothing new that would justify advancing these arguments in yesterday's rebuttal. Mr. Stringer cited document P7124, and the same document is dealt with in paragraph 320, 1203, 1232, 1255, 1310 of the Prosecution final brief, as well as in the Pusic final brief in paragraph 468 and 479. It is also a document showing that a meeting was held on 11 December 1993, but it doesn't point out any power, authority vested in Mr. Pusic. It was a meeting attended even by totally anonymous and irrelevant persons of whom we know nothing. On 11 December 1993, Mr. Pusic, as a result of this meeting, was not appointed as a member of any one commission that had the formal power to decide on prisoners in detention centres. The paragraphs on page 29923 should be 468 through 479. Yesterday we did hear something new from Mr. Stringer after all, on page 52825 through 52827, namely a rhetoric that is much milder with regard to Berislav Pusic. I quote the transcript of 1 March 2011. The Prosecutor said that Berislav Pusic no longer had exclusive powers with regard to prisoners in military prisons and that his service is co-responsible, that he was no longer -- he now no longer is in a position to do everything himself. But Mr. Stringer as at -- this actually was never the position of the Prosecution in the first place, that this was the exclusive right of Mr. Pusic. If we look at slide 6 that was part of the PowerPoint presentation here, the exchange service headed by Mr. Pusic and the commission established by Mr. Stojic on 6 August 1993 now is merely in a position of de jure responsibility. The de facto responsibility that was debated during these proceedings is no longer there. Thus, there is no more exclusiveness of Mr. Pusic as mentioned in paragraph 1190 of their final brief with regard to prisoners of war. What can I say at the end of these proceedings? I haven't heard anything about who Mr. Pusic was or what he did, and nobody else in the courtroom has heard it. We needed five years to come up with an answer to this question. Of course, that is the exclusive duty of the Prosecution. They were duty-bound to provide that answer. Certainly there is the Golden Rule in dubio pro reo, which was mentioned by my learned friend Mr. Khan and so did Mr. Sahota. The only possible conclusion is an acquittal of Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ibrisimovic. The rejoinders are now finished. We will now have a 20-minute break. And when we resume, I will give the floor to the accused if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Prlic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: For almost 20 years I fought for a modern European Bosnia and Herzegovina with equal nations and citizens. At the risk of sounding immodest, there is no one that I know of with a better record about that. The protection of this historical heritage and constitutional basis of my country was also the mission of my entire life. No one is able to question that, including during the period of the indictment. Your Honours, I'm not going to repeat my opening statement, which was entirely confirmed during my defence and even strengthened during other defence cases by new exhibits and testimonies, except that context is very important for understanding the events relating this case. When the war started, I voluntarily came back from the United States in 1992 to become a soldier. And later, I was appointed to the Special Purpose Council in Mostar. These were reasonable steps. All of us were obliged to defend our country in accordance with the system of the All People's Defence. Under the difficult circumstances of that time, there was a need to organise ourselves from bottom up and to try to stop the chaos. I was entrusted, perhaps because of my previous experiences and record, to try to help in co-ordinating the civilian parts among different municipalities and the government in Sarajevo. Such was the purpose of my appointment in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was an administrative provisional authority in the areas of more than 50 municipalities. This cannot be possibly related with the 1939 Banovina, which is presented as a territorial goal of the alleged JCE. This authority was established as a reaction to the war and as an attempt to fill in the gaps in the functioning of the newly recognised State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have to keep in mind the events as they were unfolding in and around Bosnia and Herzegovina, the challenges that emerged from the mutual collapse of all financial and social services, the lack of security at the state and local level, and the ongoing uncertainty that prevailed. The steps the Muslim side was taking added to the insecurity of the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Izetbegovic and the SDA seemed to be pursuing a policy that effectively would strip of the constituent status of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We Croats wanted to ensure that we would be enjoying full and equal rights as one of the constituent peoples in the new Bosnia and Herzegovina. We never advocated that either the Muslims or Serbs be denied their rights as constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but we insist then, as we continue to insist today, that we Croats have the rights to preserve our status, our heritage, and our culture. We were not then and we are not today Roman Catholic Bosnians. We are Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was confirmed by every international peace proposal which recognised our rights, that took part of the peace plans for the constitutional framework of a post-Yugoslavia Bosnia and Herzegovina. All the peace plans were based on the result of censuses, and none of these plans recognised any ethnic changes by force. We supported this fundamental principle and never advocated for any type of ethnic cleansing of any nation. Even in the darkest moment of the conflict, when the Croats of Central Bosnia were forced to escape for safety, we never accepted that the ancestral homes of the Croats in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be lost forever. We always expected that in the end of the war all citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were forced to leave or left out of fear would return to their homes. We never wanted less for Muslims or Serbs than we were hoping for ourselves. The work of HVO or Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is the interim executive body and later of the government of Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna. It was the most honest approach to the building of such Bosnia-Herzegovina, one that would be accepted by all its citizens. This cannot be questioned, despite some criminal activities that occurred during these times of war. By the word "honest," I mean that our goal was to protect the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina based on the reconciliation of its constituent peoples and rights of all citizens following the part of the international negotiations about its internal organisation and reacting to the events with interim measures. For internationals who came to Bosnia and Herzegovina with fixed ideas, the majority of constitutional and the organisational things were difficult to be understood, and they still are. We had [indiscernible] system that we had inherited from the former Yugoslavia. For all of us living and working in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it made sense, and we all understand -- understood the de jure authority and responsibilities that went with various institutions and positions. To those coming from Western democracies, it is obvious, then, listening to the understanding of how things worked and what the actual authority was behind titles, that little or no actual effort was made to truly understand how our system operated. It is also a fact that certain people had different ideas, like Tudjman in certain times, but one needs to look at what was happening on the ground. I met Tudjman only once in 1992, and then next during a presidential meeting in November 1993. I never heard him speaking against the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina or against the constituent rights of all free peoples or against peace or against principle of any of the proposed international peace plans. Without contacts with the leaders of Croatia, we wouldn't be able, for instance, to defend ourselves or to establish state border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The basic evidence of this attitude are the presidential transcript, but in their entirety and not by selectively picking and choosing passages out of context. I also want to point out the existence of numerous mistakes in the presidential transcripts, not to mention how easy it is to misinterpret or misuse this information. Take, for instance, in paragraph 398 in Prosecution final brief, footnote 916, where there is reference to PO 8288, where the Prosecution attributes the words to me, and a close reading of the transcript shows that someone else, unidentified, is talking. This is rather obvious when considering that the speaker says that he majored in history. This may be unintended mistake by the Prosecution, but it does serve as an example of how easy it is to misread these transcripts and perhaps draw erroneous conclusions. Your Honours, you also have all the minutes of the HVO HZ-HB meetings, which I was chairing. I urge that all be read, preferably chronologically, which would allow for context and perspective in light of the circumstances. None of the decision can be possibly linked with aims of the alleged joint criminal enterprise or with crimes themselves. I also urge you to consider my conduct, my public statement, and activities not only in relation to those minutes and decisions but also with my counterparts and the representatives of the international organisations. I did try to have positive engagement with Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, and others. Perhaps that is why I was considered as a suitable interim or acting prime minister after Medjugorje Agreement in 1993, minister of defence after the Washington Agreement, or minister of foreign affairs after Dayton Peace Accord. My activities with Prosecution Witness DZ in trying to resolve the situation in Mostar is another example. It went unnoticed because everything I was doing with DZ, my counterparts in East Mostar, and Silajdzic were secret. Not even DZ's superiors knew all the activities, let alone the other international organisation that operating on the ground. It is easy to jump to conclusions that I did almost nothing if one does not know all the facts or assumes and fixes authority upon which -- which I did not have. Hopefully, Your Honours, you have a fuller picture now that some of the facts have come out in the open and you reflect back having in mind the circumstances and placing the facts in proper context. The structures and institutions that we, the HVO HZ-HB collective, contributed to establish there was fundamental in bringing an element of formality in the organisation to the chaos that engulfed my country after the beginning of war. It was a temporary executive authority, something that was stressed at all times. Our aim was to ensure that everybody remained at their homes, that social structures, as we knew, would continue. Schools, hospitals, financial institution would function in this very chaotic and unpredictable -- unpredictable -- like King's Speech - unpredictable environment. If we failed in achieving all our goals, it was not for lack of trying. What is clear and what I do want to stress here today is that we at the HVO HZ-HB never set out to discriminate against anyone. The HVO HZ-HB was an interim executive body for civilian affairs, not a Joint Command as the Prosecutor appears to suggest. It was supposed to cease working after just several months of [indiscernible] functioning, when the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was adopted in January 1993, which would allow the position in provinces and a central government to be filled jointly with Muslims. However, there were hesitation on the Muslim side in making appointment. For instance, in Mostar, on parity basis with Croats, then the Army of BH strategically started a conflict. And as a reaction, there was a new international peace proposal for a union of free republic. Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna was set up further to this so called Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. In November 1993, the government of Croatian Republic was founded with more competent compositions, with an active parliament, and other institutions which almost immediately gave positive results. One can say that the executive structures started to function, and evidence of that are the first working programme and the budget for 1994 [indiscernible] the improvement of the overall situation. I want to stress that I don't shy away from any of the collective decisions signed on behalf of HVO HZ-HB in my capacity as its president, and I'm not avoiding any responsibility. Allow me, however, to clarify my role. I was not able to give any operative or administrative order. Both Chief of Staff testified about that. Neither to the military police nor to SIS nor to municipalities nor to anybody else, including the members of the interim executive body, and there is no evidence contrary to this. Indicative of my limited role is, for instance, that I had to ask local authorities to issue me a pass in order to be able to move around in Veli Mostar. As I said in opening statement, I never committed any crime, nor did I encourage the commission of any crime, nor am I aware of the fact that any of the members of the executive provisional body were involved in anything like this. We did everything to alleviate the consequences of war and destruction, and we took all the steps required to see the perpetrators of those crimes punished. Concretely, I have never had custody over prisoners. My function did not foresee detaining or imprisoning anyone. I didn't kept any power to release anyone. The HVO HZ-HB did not establish detention centres. It simply could not do that. And there is not evidence where the HVO HZ-HB and I as its president overstepped our de jure authority. With the orders issued by the president of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, conditions were created for the HVO HZ-HB to make a concrete contribution, improving the conditions, and finally closing the detention centres. Without this order, we were powerless to do anything, both de jure and de facto. As the president of HVO HZ-HB and the government of Croatian Republic, I did everything for the prisoners and all victims that my position and my role allowed. And those who suffered deserve sincere compassion and justice. I did try to make a positive difference, and during those times and in that environment, it was not easy. The fact that I tried to do more and my function envisaged or permitted does not mean that I had such competencies. I put myself at the disposal of anyone without a [indiscernible], from Croatia, international organisations, in the media, to bring about necessary positive changes. I've already said that I stand by all decisions of the HVO HZ-HB and later on the government of Croatian Republic, but I have often asked myself if this situation happened again, would I do anything different or maybe did I omit to do something? I have found nothing, having in my circumstances. In that period, I could have left, escaped, and avoided the indictment, but in that case I would have been guilty to myself my entire life because I failed to do something in order to improve the situation. Who would have benefitted from my leaving? I stayed so that I could look everyone in the eye and could continue working on the project of building a modern, independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a project to which I devoted most of my life. How could I accept the thesis that I occupied my own country for which I was among the very first, as people said, who already in 1990 was in favour of its independence? I held many governmental positions in Bosnia and Herzegovina as its vice-president and acting president until 1991 and then from 1994 until 2003. First as minister of defence for Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that I was entrusted with overseeing the activities of both the Army of BH and HVO while the war continued, all the way up to the Dayton Peace Accord. And all in that small area where people knew, as they say, who was shooting at whom. After all, for all those who had left their homes in any manner, the governments to which I was a member ensured their return and the return of their property. I repeat, for all, no matter of their national affiliation, including from the municipalities mentioned in the indictment. As the head of practically the only functioning ministry in state, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for Bosnia and Herzegovina, I represented for more than five years all of its citizens, including the victims of these times of war. Throughout all these position, I have supported project of international justice. Despite almost seven years in custody, despite all speeches of my accusers, I still trust this Tribunal is able to bring justice, as I believed in all those years since 1993. Your Honours, you have the evidence before you. I ask that you not succumb to any [indiscernible] or final briefs. Examine carefully all the testimonies and all the evidence. Please turn to the realistic context of the entirety of the events. I am confident that with that approach you will succeed in making a fair and objective decision. Thank you, Your Honours, for your understanding and for the very hard force you have put thus far into this case and for all the hard work that practically lies ahead of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stojic is now going to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED STOJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Your Honours, I've not prepared a speech. I've not prepared any notes. I'm going to speak from my heart and from my soul. I'll share with you my feelings, and I did not need to prepare for that. There are just a few things that I would like to share with everybody. First of all, Your Honours, I would like to thank you for your understanding, when you did me favours and let me go home to my family. My family also has to bear the same burden that I've been bearing for five or six years. Your Honours, you know that as soon as I was indicted I surrendered myself to this Tribunal. I respect the Tribunal. I respect you, Your Honours. And I will respect every decision as I have done in the past. For example, when you granted me provisional release, I respected that. And I believe that you didn't have any objections to the way I met the conditions of my provisional release, because I did it fully. Throughout the trial I've been present in the courtroom. I believe that only myself and His Honour Judge Antonetti have been in the courtroom every day, day in, day out. There were even situations when I presented myself running a fever. My lawyers know that only too well, but I was present every second of the trial. Your Honours, as far as the judgement is concerned, there is just one thing that I would like to ask you. I know that you have a lot of documents to study. I've studied all the documents over the last six or seven years. I have left no stone unturned with my lawyers. And it was not easy to do it. And I'm sure that it will not be easy for you either. But please read everything. Read the transcript. It -- read all the documents. Look at all the facts and render your judgement based on that. Your Honours, this is what I have to say in open session: Whatever your decision may be, I will honour it to the very last word, because you're honourable people, you're good Judges, and you are doing your job well. Second of all, I would like to thank my Defence team for the understanding they showed to me during these proceedings. They have been very understanding towards myself, towards my family. They've always found time to talk to my family, to my wife, to my children, and to my parents. I would like to thank them for the hard work that they've done over the past five years. And I have to tell you, Your Honours, that whatever they have told you during the proceedings, in their closing arguments, all that had been agreed with me, and I stand behind every one of their words. Your Honours, I also wanted to say at the very end one of the most important things, and those are the victims of this war. The hardest moments in my life were when I listened to these people, when I looked at them here in the courtroom. Your Honours, I assure you that there's no document, that there is no proof of my conduct that contributed to any of the crimes. I never ordered any crimes. I never condoned any crimes. And I know that there were crimes. I've -- I've seen that in the courtroom. Your Honours, from the bottom of my heart, I would like to say that I sympathise. I feel compassion for those people, for the victims of the war that happened down there, and especially the Muslim victims of that war. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your patience. This is all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now giving the floor to the last accused who wishes to speak. I believe this is General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everybody in courtroom, and especially to you, Your Honours. Although I was a professional soldier, a career soldier who had been trained for warfare, my nature is entirely different. I really believe that it is better to talk and negotiate, to reach a peaceful agreement on any of the disputes than wage war, albeit for a day, and this is what I advocated in mid-1993, and I still advocate that. My opinion hasn't changed. However, war, unfortunately, was unavoidable in the former Yugoslavia as it was at the time. When I was a member of the JNA before the war, I never even dreamt that the peoples of Yugoslavia could wage a war against each other, and it never occurred to me that the main force that would start the wheels of war turning might be the Yugoslav People's Army, an army that I had served in for 20 years. Unfortunately, the JNA waged that war in the interest of only one people of the former Yugoslavia and we know only too well which people was that. When the things started, I knew what to do. I didn't have anything to do with Serbia. My homeland was Croatia. And it is only normal that I decided to help my own state, my own Republic of Croatia. During the course of that war, my destiny also took me to the south of Croatia. That was at the greatest peril at that time. In 1992, UNPROFOR was already was between the warring sides in the most Croatia but not in the south, which means that Croatia had a tacit right to try and liberate its southern part. That's why I joined the command in Blace -- in Ploce. I joined all the others in their effort to march towards Dubrovnik and liberate that part of Croatia. Initially, we wanted to prevent the occupation of larger territories. Unfortunately, all the attacks were launched from the republic which had the longest border with Croatia and that's Bosnia. And it was not the Muslim people that launched attacks against the Republic of Croatia. Those were the units of the JNA which had been brought over from Serbia and that had been transferred from Slovenia and Croatia, and they were the ones that had to be countered. And we stopped them. We stopped their onslaught in the valley of the Neretva River. Just as we were getting ready to march towards Dubrovnik, they had their own ideas, and that's when Kupres happened in the month of April 1993. More powerful and better equipped, the JNA overpowered the HVO in Kupres. They threatened Livno, Kupres, Tomislavgrad, and the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia from Sinj to the Neretva valley. Your Honours, in that part of the Croatian border there was no single Croatian soldier. The way we saw things was that the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina would manage to stop the JNA, that they would -- the JNA would not be allowed to get to Bosnia and Herzegovina or through Bosnia and Herzegovina down to the Republic of Croatia. But the situation was different. We had to stop our efforts to liberate the south of Croatia and instead to help the HVO forces, which by then were still not well organised. And I repeat, only the HVO forces. When I arrived there in April, there was no other formation there. There was no other army presence there. Fortunately enough, with our help the HVO managed to save Livno, Tomislavgrad, and Prozor. And never again was the JNA capable of posing a serious threat in the Livno theatre of war. Let me tell you that I spoke to the commander of those forces, the OG in Kupres. The commander was General Galic. I asked him what his opinion was about the attacks against the HVO and their onslaughts towards the territory of the Republic of Croatia. When that problem was solved, we had to solve the problem that existed in the Neretva valley. The problem was major, and the HVO was a small military. Truth be told, along the border of the Republic of Croatia they did have the assistance of the Croatian Army. All that was resolved in June 1993, and this was the first large area that the forces that fought against the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina managed to liberate. And those were the forces of the HVO with quite a large participation of Muslim people among their ranks. Those people volunteered and joined the HVO of their own will. And let's not forget that there was also an organised force of the then-government, the independent Mostar Battalion and its 350 soldiers. So that was part of the organised BiH Army. Therefore, I went to counter the attacks of Serbia -- Serbs in Bosnia. That's how I wished to help the defence of the Republic of Croatia as well as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Without that fight, without that assistance, Bosnia and Herzegovina would have lost all touch with the outer world. That part of the Republic of Croatia, that border south of Split down to the Neretva valley, is the only connection of the free part of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the world. At least that was the situation then. Life was difficult there, but still there was life. And I'm proud that we managed to maintain that area, to make it viable, to make it functionable, to make it passable, to keep the free passage from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia and from there even further, both from Croats and Muslims who resided in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. I was one of those who created the Croatian Defence Council. I used my knowledge from the JNA and the Croatian Army that I had gathered thus far. And I repeat once again, neither myself nor anybody else never prevented a Muslim soldier who wanted to become a member of the Croatian Defence Council from doing so. They joined us in their hundreds. We accepted them, we equipped them, we armed them, and together with them we waged the same war. In the month of February, I wrote a letter to Sefer Halilovic, and I told him that I rejoice every new soldier, a Croat and Muslim alike, because all of us would fight together. And I also told him in that letter that I was happy that his commander Ali Pasalic understood the situation and accepted, as he put it himself, Petkovic as commander in that area. He said, There are very few of us; we do not have the power; and I will be in command in Konjic because there I have more power than you do. And we accepted that fact. That's how we did until the month of April 1993. There are numerous orders speaking to that effect, about Pasalic reporting to me, about measures that he took, how he ordered his brigades, either the Mostar Brigade or the Bregava Brigade, and all the other units under his command. Incidents and misunderstandings started sometime in April, and they became more frequent and lasted longer. I claim that I did all that I could, together with Sefer Halilovic and Arif Pasalic, to establish the relationship of trust and co-operation. Your Honours, you heard, and I'll try to briefly summarise what happened from the 18th of April 1993 until the moment when Halilovic left his position, I'll try to tell you what we did, and I admit that it was done with the help of the international community. On the 18th of April, Mr. Boban and Mr. Izetbegovic issued a statement that conflicts had to be stopped. General Krnovas [phoen] came to Mostar at that time. Mr. Thebault came to Mostar, Mr. Ganic came, a member of the Presidency of Croat -- his name escapes me. Oh, yes, Boras. I was there as well, Pasalic was there, Mr. Prlic was there. And we agreed on that day that we would resolve the situation in Mostar. And Halilovic was supposed to arrive and attend the meeting because that's what Mr. Izetbegovic had promised us. Zagreb, Halilovic did arrive, together with Mr. Morillion, on the 19th of April. They flew to Mostar, and they joined the team. On the 19th, we toured Mostar. We inspected the area together. And then we decided that General Pellnas would work together with the Mostar Group and cover the area from Mostar to Konjic and that the rest of us, led by General Morillon and Mr. Thebault, should set out to Central Bosnia. We arrived in Zenica and you saw that that on the 20th we, firstly, despite fierce arguments, we issued an argument [as interpreted] where it says on the bullet point 1 that we were members of the same army. The document was testified by both Mr. Thebault and Mr. Morillon. They put their signatures on the document. A lot of support to that document was issued by Mr. Ganic, the then-president of the Presidency who was with us, and Mr. Zubak, who was a member of our delegation. On the following day, after we spent the entire night telephoning to all command levels to tell them that we wanted a complete cease-fire, after a short stay in the British Battalion, we spent the entire following day touring the most threatened areas. Myself, Halilovic, and all the other men who were with us. And for that I'm eternally grateful to the British Battalion who took us to every single point where we wanted to go. And we managed. We managed to deal with the situation in Central Bosnia. And on the following day we continued, and then we received an invitation on the 24th to report to Zagreb or, rather, to be in Zagreb on the 24th at that a meeting would take place there. So Mr. Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, myself, and Halilovic we went to Zagreb to discuss the situation further. In Zagreb we confirmed by way of a statement that we were a single army and the two of us signed a statement about a Joint Command that had to be established and that we accepted that. And as we accepted all that, we returned to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then on the 28th, immediately after that, three days thereafter, with the help of Mr. Thebault, we arrived in Jablanica. We tried to agree as to what should be done in Jablanica and Konjic when it was their turn. And then we continued towards Zenica. On the 28th we were in Zenica, on the 29th and the 30th we stayed in the area, in the general area. We established the Joint Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You had an occasion to listen to Filipovic, my representative the Croatian Defence Council, and you also saw a list of the people whom I delegated into the Joint Staff. You saw that my intentions were good. I faxed the same document to Lord Owen, to show him that our intentions were serious. This is what we did. We established a Joint Staff. And then on the 29th and the 30th of April, we issued our first orders. It was myself and Halilovic who issued them, but the heading read, The Joint Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the official heading. I signed the documents on behalf of the joint forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the 30th of April, we agreed that due to certain commitments that Halilovic had in other parts of the theatre of war that concerned the Serbs that we should met in Jablanica. And then on the 4th and 5th of May we did arrive in Jablanica. After a very hard meeting, we again started to tour the area in order to resolve the matters on the ground as much as we could at that moment. At that time, unfortunately, the 9th of May happened. You heard the arguments proposed both the Prosecution and the Defence. It's up to you to decide what happened there. However, on the 10th of May, pursuant to the agreement by Izetbegovic and Boban, I was in Kiseljak. On the 11th, I was joined by Halilovic.
