And I think it was only normal for us to return where it was dangerous and that was the Neretva valley. And then we arrived in Medjugorje. You all saw documents, but let me say that we were together on the 12th, on the 13th, on the 14th. We were together with the representatives of international organisations and we were all there in order to deal with very concrete problems. And I admit that those were not minor problems. We were not sitting in the command in Medjugorje. We toured the area just as before. And then already on the 18th, again upon the invitation of the president, we found ourselves in Medjugorje. Mr. Prlic also mentioned that date. He told you what was agreed there. Myself and Halilovic remained together on the 19th, then in Mostar on the 20th and the 21st of May. Again on the 21st of May we were in Konjic and Jablanica. We were there in order to try and deal with very specific problems on the ground. And let me continue. A short interruption ensued. And then on the 28th of May we found ourselves in Sarajevo, myself and him, as well as the gentleman from UNPROFOR. I assert, Your Honours, that if we -- we managed to place the situation under a tolerable control. However, what happened after that was Travnik, the beginning of June. The HVO was attacked in Travnik. It -- and 20.000 Croats scattered in different directions. On the 9th of June, I was invited by the international community to arrange a meeting in Kiseljak with Halilovic. I arrived. I waited. And I learned from General Morillon that Rasim Delic on that day was standing in for Halilovic or, rather, replaced Halilovic on the day. He asked me to stay. He asked me to wait until Delic arrived in Kiseljak. Delic did arrive in Kiseljak on the 10th. You have that document, we signed that document, it was an agreement of sorts; however, what Halilovic had done before him, Delic never did. Delic said that he had only assumed his duties and that he had to return to the command in Sarajevo in order to be briefed by his own men, and Travnik remained out of his focus, as it were. Truth be told, under bullet point 2 we said that we would brief members of the Joint Staff about everything. To be honest, unofficial -- unofficial stories and rumours according to which Halilovic was a bosom buddy with Petkovic and that the two of them together were preventing the BH Army from achieving further successes; I don't know who spread those rumours, but once again you have to look what was happening between the 18th of April to the 9th of June. Maybe for five or six days that wasn't true, but the rest of the time Halilovic and I were always there in the areas where fighting was going on. This was the only way we knew how to prevent the evil from getting out of proportions and spreading even further. That was our way to fight it. In my orders to my subordinates, I tried to instruct them, to guide them, to refer them to their colleagues in the BiH Army, to negotiate, to find compromises, to refer to our agreements and accords. Your Honours, I had my hands full. And I'm sure that, faced with so many things that I had to deal with, I may have made mistakes. I don't know what I would do today in a similar situation. It's very difficult for me to say. I'm sure that I would treat certain things in a different way, but I can claim that I was very sincere when I spoke to Halilovic and Pasalic, that I didn't have a hidden agenda. Your Honours, I would be very happy if this story that I just shared with you, when I talked to people, when I toured the grounds, if that had saved lives. And I believe that I did save lives, not just myself but Mr. Halilovic who was there with me. Unfortunately, my new counterpart Delic didn't like that approach. He never went to Bugojno, Fojnica, or anywhere else. He just wasn't keen. He didn't want to go anywhere. He just waited for me to come to Sarajevo to come to him to sign documents, and that was so unlike Sefer Halilovic, who was always there. Your Honours, crimes were never what I wanted. I never planned or agreed on committing any crimes with anybody. My Defence team and myself have tried to explain all of my actions to you, Your Honours, and especially those who are in greatest dispute. And I had the courage to sit in front of you and answer all the questions that you had to put to me. During the proceedings I asked the floor in order to help you get to the truth, to make this -- these proceedings as expeditious as possible, not only for my sake but for the sake of everybody else. I believe that you are going to study all the documents in their integrity. You are professional Judges. I do not have any doubt that your decision will be just and fair. I take this opportunity to apologise to all the victims of actions and omissions committed by any members of the HVO, and I apologise in particular to Muslims, to those Bosniaks with whom I started defending Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. I am sorry that the unity of the peoples did not last throughout the war, for four years. And that for almost 12 years we were enemies in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- for almost 12 months. I would like to say that in 1994, from the then-leaders of the HVO I was proposed as the Chief of the Main Staff, and we -- I did that and worked on the implementation of the Split Agreement and other agreement that had been issued by then. Your Honours, I would like to thank you for always being benevolent towards my humanitarian requests. Thank you for allowing me to be treated in the Republic of Croatia. And the only times I was absent from the courtroom was when I was ill. And this is all, Your Honours, that I thought I should say in my final address. I would like to thank you for your patience, for your efforts, for your understanding shown to all us over the past five years. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the accused who have wanted to speak have done so. Let me read out Rule 87(A) of the Rules: "Following the parties' closing arguments, the Presiding Judge brings the proceedings to a close, and the Trial Chamber will then deliberate in camera. The accused will only be found guilty if the Trial Chamber is of the view that their guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt." I see that I can take note of the fact that the closing arguments have been done. I now adjourn the hearing sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: sine die

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.44 p.m.
